questions.stem: A student asks why viruses are excluded from the traditional definition of living organisms, given that they carry genetic material and evolve over time. Which of the following best explains why viruses are not considered truly alive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are destroyed by ordinary environmental exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are made only of lipid, with no protein at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are too small to be seen by any microscope

choices.label: D
choices.text: They cannot reproduce without taking over a host cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: They contain no genetic code of their own

explanation.summary: Viruses straddle the line between living and nonliving because they cannot replicate outside a host cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viruses are small particles of genetic code, lipids, and proteins that must commandeer a living cell's machinery to reproduce. Because they cannot reproduce on their own, they are not considered truly alive. Being nonliving does not keep them from being one of the greatest problems in modern medicine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Non-enveloped viruses are in fact quite stable in the environment, so fragility is not the criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: All viruses have a protein coat called a capsid; the lipid envelope is the optional component.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viruses are too small for light microscopes, but small size is not what excludes them from being alive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Every virus carries a genome of either DNA or RNA; having no genetic code is not the issue.

questions.stem: A virus recovered from a contaminated countertop several days after it was deposited is found to have no lipid bilayer surrounding its capsid. Which of the following is most likely true of this virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is readily inactivated by ethanol-based hand sanitizer

choices.label: B
choices.text: It must carry reverse transcriptase inside the virion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its capsid is helical rather than icosahedral in shape

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its capsid is icosahedral and it is environmentally stable

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its genome must consist of double-stranded DNA

explanation.summary: All non-enveloped viruses are icosahedral and are stable in the environment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capsids are either icosahedral or helical, and viruses lacking an envelope are always icosahedral. Without a lipid envelope to dry out or dissolve, these virions persist on surfaces, which is exactly why one was still recoverable days later.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ethanol works by dissolving a lipid envelope, so naked viruses resist it rather than succumb to it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcriptase is the hallmark of retroviruses, not of non-enveloped viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helical capsids are found in enveloped viruses; a naked virus is icosahedral.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Envelope status says nothing about the genome; naked viruses may carry DNA or RNA.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of a newly released virion shows a lipid bilayer studded with surface proteins surrounding the capsid. This lipid bilayer is most directly derived from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipid synthesized de novo by virally encoded enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Membrane of the host cell from which it budded

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum lipoproteins that adsorb onto the capsid surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: The peptidoglycan wall of a co-infecting bacterium

choices.label: E
choices.text: The protein capsid itself, which flattens into a sheet

explanation.summary: A viral envelope is a lipid bilayer taken from the host cell membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some viruses are covered by an envelope, which is usually a remnant of cell membrane from the host cell. Newly assembled virions move to the cell membrane and form an envelope from it as they bud outward, which is how influenza and RSV acquire their envelopes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viruses take a membrane from the host rather than synthesizing bilayer lipid themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The envelope is an organized bilayer acquired during budding, not adsorbed serum lipid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptidoglycan is a bacterial cell wall polymer and is not part of any viral particle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsid is a protein coat that sits inside the envelope; it is not a lipid structure.

questions.stem: A virology text groups the clinically important viruses into DNA viruses, RNA viruses, and retroviruses. Which of the following best describes the genome of the DNA virus group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All DNA viruses carry their own RNA replicase enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: All DNA viruses package a segmented RNA genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: All DNA viruses use a single-stranded DNA genome

choices.label: D
choices.text: All use double-stranded DNA except parvovirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Half use double-stranded and half single-stranded DNA

explanation.summary: DNA viruses use double-stranded DNA, with parvovirus the single-stranded exception.
explanation.whyCorrect: All DNA viruses use dsDNA except parvovirus, which is single stranded. Whatever the strandedness, the genome must first be transcribed into messenger RNA before viral replication can proceed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RNA replicase is introduced by (−)ssRNA viruses, not by DNA viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: By definition DNA viruses use DNA, not RNA, as their genome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Single-stranded DNA is the exception, seen with parvovirus, not the rule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The split is far from even; dsDNA is the near-universal pattern among DNA viruses.

questions.stem: Almost all RNA viruses package a single-stranded RNA genome. Which of the following groups is the exception that uses double-stranded RNA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpesviruses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parvoviruses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Poxviruses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reoviruses

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retroviruses

explanation.summary: Reoviruses are the double-stranded RNA exception among RNA viruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Almost all RNA viruses use ssRNA, but reoviruses use dsRNA. These viruses introduce multiple RNA molecules that code for multiple proteins once inside the host cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpesviruses are dsDNA viruses known for establishing latent infections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parvovirus is the single-stranded DNA virus, not an RNA virus at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Poxviruses are dsDNA viruses, notable instead for replicating in the cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retroviruses are (+)ssRNA viruses that carry reverse transcriptase, not dsRNA viruses.

questions.stem: The purified genome of a (+)ssRNA virus is added to a cell-free system containing ribosomes, transfer RNAs, and amino acids. Viral protein is produced with no intervening nucleic acid step. Which property of (+)ssRNA best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It carries a polymerase covalently attached to each end

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a template that must first be copied into (−)ssRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is double stranded and unwinds inside the ribosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is equivalent to mRNA and can be translated directly

choices.label: E
choices.text: It must be reverse transcribed into DNA before any use

explanation.summary: Sense, or (+)ssRNA, is equivalent to mRNA and is translated straight to protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Single-stranded sense RNA has the same polarity as messenger RNA, so host ribosomes read it directly without forming an intermediate molecule. This is why only ribosomes and building blocks are needed for protein to appear in the system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No attached polymerase is needed, since the host ribosome does the translating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is antisense (−)ssRNA that must first be copied into (+)ssRNA, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: (+)ssRNA is single stranded by definition; dsRNA is the reovirus pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcription into DNA is the retroviral strategy and is not required here.

questions.stem: A (−)ssRNA virus uncoats inside a host cell. Before any viral protein can be produced, which of the following must occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Host DNA polymerase must copy the genome into cDNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: RNA replicase must copy the genome into (+)ssRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: The genome must be carried into the nucleolus by importins

choices.label: D
choices.text: The genome must be cleaved into several smaller ssRNA segments

choices.label: E
choices.text: The genome must be integrated into host chromosomal DNA

explanation.summary: Antisense (−)ssRNA must be transcribed to (+)ssRNA by RNA replicase before translation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most (−)ssRNA viruses introduce RNA replicase, also called RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which forms (+)ssRNA from the antisense genome. That (+)ssRNA then behaves like mRNA and is translated into protein by host ribosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Copying RNA into cDNA requires reverse transcriptase, which these viruses do not carry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm; nuclear import is not the prerequisite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Segmenting the genome is not a required step for protein production here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Integration into the host genome is a retroviral step carried out by integrase.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma is enrolled in a trial of an antiviral agent that inhibits viral RNA replicase within infected cells. This drug would be expected to work best against which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A double-stranded DNA virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: A double-stranded DNA-RT virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A retrovirus that carries reverse transcriptase

choices.label: D
choices.text: A single-stranded DNA virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: An antisense single-stranded RNA virus

explanation.summary: RNA replicase is the enzyme (−)ssRNA viruses must introduce to make (+)ssRNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: A drug aimed at RNA replicase blocks the step in which antisense RNA is copied into (+)ssRNA. Without that copy the virus cannot produce the mRNA-equivalent it needs to code for viral components, so replication of a (−)ssRNA virus halts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: dsDNA viruses use host transcription machinery to make mRNA and need no RNA replicase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: dsDNA-RT viruses carry their own polymerase for RNA intermediates rather than RNA replicase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Retroviruses depend on reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA, a different enzyme target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ssDNA viruses replicate much as dsDNA viruses do, again without RNA replicase.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV infection. Which enzyme carried within the HIV virion converts the viral RNA genome into a DNA copy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Host RNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neuraminidase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA replicase

explanation.summary: Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase, which produces DNA from their RNA genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV is a (+)ssRNA retrovirus. Reverse transcriptase transcribes its RNA into DNA, the reverse of the usual flow of genetic information, and the resulting DNA transcript is then read by the infected cell as if it were host DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Host RNA polymerase transcribes DNA into RNA, the opposite of what is needed here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Integrase inserts the DNA copy into the host genome after reverse transcription has occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neuraminidase is not the enzyme responsible for copying a retroviral genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RNA replicase makes (+)ssRNA from antisense RNA and is used by (−)ssRNA viruses.

questions.stem: After reverse transcriptase produces a DNA copy of the HIV genome, that DNA is inserted into the chromosome of the infected cell. Which viral enzyme performs this insertion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neuraminidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peptidyl transferase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA replicase

explanation.summary: Integrase splices the reverse-transcribed viral DNA into the host genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make DNA and then integrate that DNA into the host genome using integrase. Host machinery subsequently replicates the virus from the integrated DNA, which is why HIV becomes a permanent part of the infected cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuraminidase is not involved in inserting viral DNA into host chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptidyl transferase is a ribosomal activity of protein synthesis, not of integration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase performs the preceding step, producing the DNA copy from RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RNA replicase forms (+)ssRNA from (−)ssRNA and plays no role in integration.

questions.stem: A virion has attached to a respiratory epithelial cell, has been taken into the cell, and has just shed its protein coat, releasing its nucleic acid and enzymes. Which step of the viral life cycle occurs next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assembly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attachment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penetration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replication

explanation.summary: The six steps proceed attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication, assembly, release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shedding the protein coat is uncoating, the third step. Replication follows, in which viral nucleic acids, enzymes, and proteins are copied using host machinery, before the new components are assembled into virions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assembly of new virions comes after the components have been replicated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Attachment to a surface receptor is the first step and has already occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penetration, entry into the cell, has already happened before uncoating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Release of mature virions is the final step of the cycle.

questions.stem: An influenza virion bound to receptors on an airway epithelial cell is drawn inside the cell. In the general scheme of viral infection, penetration occurs by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endocytosis or fusion of the viral envelope with the membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Injection of the genome through a rigid tail structure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passive diffusion of the intact virion across the membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phagocytosis carried out only by tissue macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transport through nuclear pores set in the plasma membrane

explanation.summary: Viruses penetrate cells either by endocytosis or by fusing their envelope with the cell membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viral attachment to the cell surface allows entry through two general mechanisms: receptor-mediated endocytosis, in which the virus signals the cell to engulf it, and fusion of the viral envelope with the cell membrane, which releases the capsid into the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Genome injection through a tail is a bacteriophage device, not the general mechanism described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Virions are far too large and polar-coated to diffuse passively across a bilayer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Entry is not restricted to macrophages; any cell bearing the right receptor can be penetrated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nuclear pores sit in the nuclear envelope, not in the plasma membrane.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with 3 days of fever, irritability, and refusal to eat. Examination shows swollen, erythematous gums and multiple painful vesicles and shallow ulcers on the lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa. After this illness resolves, the responsible virus will persist for life at which of the following sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and some epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes, macrophages, and marrow progenitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: Herpetic gingivostomatitis is a primary HSV-1 infection, and HSV-1 becomes latent in sensory ganglia, most commonly the trigeminal ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Painful swollen gums with vesicular and ulcerative lesions in and around the mouth of a child is the classic picture of herpetic gingivostomatitis, which the brick attributes to initial infection with HSV-1. HSV-1 travels from the mucocutaneous site of inoculation up peripheral sensory nerves and establishes latency in sensory ganglia, most commonly the trigeminal ganglia. The illness itself resolves in 2-3 weeks, but the latent virus remains and can reactivate as herpes labialis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes (and some epithelial cells) are where Epstein-Barr virus, HHV-4, establishes latency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 T lymphocytes are the latency site of HHV-6 and HHV-7, the agents of roseola infantum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells harbor latent cytomegalovirus, HHV-5.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sacral ganglia are the usual latency site of HSV-2, which causes genital rather than oral disease.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had three episodes in 2 years of painful genital ulcers, each preceded by a day of tingling. PCR of a lesion swab is positive for herpes simplex virus type 2. Between these episodes, where does the virus reside?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes of the regional lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow hematopoietic progenitor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neurons of the cranial nerve ganglia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: HSV-2 establishes latency in sensory ganglia, most commonly the sacral ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-2 is inoculated at genital mucosa and is carried by retrograde transport up the peripheral sensory nerves that serve that territory, which drain to the sacral dorsal root ganglia. The virus remains latent there and, on reactivation, travels back down the same nerves to produce recurrent genital lesions. This is the mirror image of HSV-1, which uses the trigeminal ganglia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes are the latency reservoir for Epstein-Barr virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow progenitor cells harbor cytomegalovirus, not herpes simplex virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cranial nerve ganglia, along with dorsal root ganglia, are latency sites for varicella zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The trigeminal ganglia serve the face and are the usual latency site for HSV-1, not genital HSV-2.

questions.stem: Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4) persists for the life of the host after primary infection. Which of the following is its primary site of latency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and some epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circulating monocytes and tissue macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: EBV (HHV-4) is the herpesvirus that establishes latency primarily in B lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick groups the human herpesviruses by where each establishes latency. EBV is unusual among them in choosing a lymphoid reservoir: it primarily becomes latent in B lymphocytes, although it can also be found in epithelial cells and other cell types. This lymphotropism is why EBV disease is dominated by lymphoid rather than neurologic findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 T lymphocytes are the latency site of HHV-6 and HHV-7.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes and macrophages, together with bone marrow progenitors, harbor latent cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sacral dorsal root ganglia are the usual latency site of HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trigeminal sensory ganglia harbor latent HSV-1.

questions.stem: Cytomegalovirus reactivates in a kidney transplant recipient who is receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Before reactivation, the latent viral genomes in this patient were most likely carried in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and mucosal epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes, macrophages, and marrow progenitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus (HHV-5) establishes latency in monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists CMV as establishing latency in various cells including monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells. Because the reservoir is myeloid rather than neuronal, reactivating CMV can seed many organs through the circulation rather than reappearing in one dermatome or at one mucocutaneous site. Immunosuppression, as in transplantation, is the classic trigger for reactivation of any herpesvirus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes and epithelial cells are the reservoir for Epstein-Barr virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 T lymphocytes harbor latent HHV-6 and HHV-7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sacral dorsal root ganglia harbor latent HSV-2, the usual cause of genital herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trigeminal ganglia are the latency site of HSV-1, which reactivates as cold sores.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant has 3 days of high fever followed by a rose-colored rash that appears as the fever breaks. The illness is attributed to human herpesvirus 6. This virus establishes latency in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and mucosal epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes and bone marrow progenitor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: HHV-6 and HHV-7 cause roseola infantum and establish latency in CD4 T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies HHV-6 and HHV-7 as the agents of roseola infantum, a childhood illness of high fever followed by rash, and states that these viruses establish latency in CD4 T cells. This places them apart from the neurotropic alpha herpesviruses and from the myeloid reservoir used by CMV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes and epithelial cells are the reservoir for Epstein-Barr virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes and bone marrow progenitors are the reservoir for cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia are the latency sites of varicella zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV-1 uses the trigeminal ganglia; it causes oral lesions, not a febrile exanthem of infancy.

questions.stem: A newly isolated virus is assigned to the family Herpesviridae. Which of the following genome and particle descriptions should be expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circular double-stranded DNA, naked, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linear double-stranded DNA, enveloped, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Linear positive-sense RNA, enveloped, helical capsid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linear single-stranded DNA, naked, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Segmented single-stranded RNA, enveloped, helical capsid

explanation.summary: All herpesviruses are enveloped, icosahedral virions carrying a linear double-stranded DNA genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that all herpesviruses store their genetic information as linear double-stranded DNA and have an enveloped, icosahedral capsid, with replication occurring in the host nucleus. These shared structural features are what unify an otherwise clinically diverse family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpesvirus DNA is linear, not circular, and the virion is enveloped rather than naked.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herpesviruses do not have an RNA genome, and their capsid symmetry is icosahedral rather than helical.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The herpesvirus genome is double-stranded, and herpesvirus particles carry an envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Herpesviruses are DNA viruses; a segmented RNA genome with helical symmetry describes a different family entirely.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of a cell infected with a herpesvirus shows budding nucleocapsids acquiring an envelope at a site unusual for enveloped viruses. From which membrane is the herpesvirus envelope derived?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cisternal membrane of the Golgi apparatus

choices.label: B
choices.text: The limiting membrane of host cell lysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nuclear membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: The outer mitochondrial membrane of the host cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The plasma membrane of the infected host cell

explanation.summary: Herpesvirus nucleocapsids become enveloped by pinching off a segment of the nuclear membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick highlights this as the odd feature of herpesviruses: budding nucleocapsids of new virions become enveloped by pinching off a segment of the nuclear membrane, whereas most enveloped viruses take their envelope from the host cell membrane. The enveloped virions then accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum and are transported out of the cell to infect surrounding cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Golgi is part of the export route for many viral glycoproteins but is not where the herpesvirus envelope is acquired.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysosomal membranes are degradative compartments and are not a source of viral envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondrial membranes are not used by any human virus as an envelope source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The plasma membrane is the source of the envelope for most other enveloped viruses, which is precisely the contrast the brick draws.

questions.stem: An antiviral compound is designed to inhibit replication of the herpes simplex virus genome. To reach its target, the drug must be active in which of the following compartments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytoplasmic membranous replication factories

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endosomal vesicles near the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lumen of the rough endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: D
choices.text: The matrix of host cell mitochondria

choices.label: E
choices.text: The nucleus of the infected host cell

explanation.summary: Herpesvirus replication occurs in the host cell nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the virus is transported to a nuclear pore, its DNA is released into the nucleus, and the brick states that replication of all herpesviruses occurs in the host nucleus. A drug targeting genome replication must therefore act on nuclear events. The endoplasmic reticulum is involved later, when assembled virions accumulate there before export.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic replication complexes are used by many RNA viruses, not by herpesviruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endosomes participate in entry for some viruses but are not where herpesvirus DNA is copied.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Virions accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum after assembly, but the genome is not replicated there.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mitochondrial matrix has no role in herpesvirus genome replication.

questions.stem: After replicating in oral epithelium, herpes simplex virus enters sensory nerve endings and travels to the neuronal cell body, where it becomes latent. Which receptor interaction and which direction of axonal transport best describe this step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neurokinin-1 receptor with anterograde transport

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neurokinin-1 receptor with retrograde transport

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor with anterograde transport

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor with retrograde transport

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin receptor with retrograde transport

explanation.summary: HSV binds the neurokinin-1 receptor and moves up peripheral sensory nerves by retrograde transport to establish latency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that herpes simplex virus establishes latent infection in neurons by binding the neurokinin-1 receptor and migrating up the peripheral sensory nerves from the site of initial exposure, which is retrograde transport. Once in the cell body, the virus is carried to a nuclear pore and its DNA is released into the nucleus, where it can remain latent for years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The receptor is correct, but anterograde transport moves virus away from the ganglion toward the skin, which is what happens later during reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is not the entry receptor described for HSV, and anterograde transport is the direction used on reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retrograde transport is correct, but the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is not the receptor the brick attributes to HSV neuronal entry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The transferrin receptor mediates iron uptake and is not the receptor used by HSV to enter neurons.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops a cold sore on his lower lip several days after a ski trip. Which of the following best describes how virus latent in his trigeminal ganglion produced this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enters the blood and seeds the lip through dermal capillaries

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is carried to the lip within infected circulating monocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is shed into saliva and reinfects the lip from outside

choices.label: D
choices.text: It moves down sensory nerves and infects flanking epithelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It passes from neuron to neuron across the facial dermis

explanation.summary: Reactivated HSV travels back down peripheral sensory nerves and destroys the epithelial cells flanking the nerve endings.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes reactivation as the reverse of latency establishment: once reactivated, HSV travels back down the peripheral sensory nerves by anterograde transport and infects flanking epithelial cells, leading to their destruction. Because HSV-1 and HSV-2 replicate rapidly and are cytolytic, this epithelial destruction produces the visible vesicle and subsequent ulcer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viremic seeding of the lip is not the mechanism of recurrent herpes labialis; the virus travels within nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transport inside mononuclear cells is how varicella zoster virus reaches the skin during chicken pox, not how HSV recurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recurrences arise from latent virus already in the ganglion, not from external reinoculation of the lip.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spread from neuron to neuron through the dermis is not described; the virus moves within the axons of sensory nerves.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old medical student develops a cold sore during final examinations; a previous outbreak followed a severe sunburn. Which of the following best explains why her latent virus began replicating on both occasions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic therapy eliminated the protective normal oral flora

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete loss of antibody allowed the virus to return to the lip

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutation of the viral genome during latency restored replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reinfection from a new contact introduced a second viral strain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stress, immunosuppression, and tissue damage trigger reactivation

explanation.summary: Herpesviruses reactivate when the host is stressed, immunocompromised, has another infection, or sustains tissue damage such as sunburn or trauma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states directly that the virus can rapidly replicate when the host is stressed, immunocompromised, has other infections, or receives tissue damage from infections, sunburns, or trauma. Both of this student's triggers, examination stress and a sunburn, appear on that list. Nothing about the latent genome itself changes; what changes is the host state that had been containing it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of normal bacterial flora is not one of the reactivation triggers described for herpesviruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody does not disappear between outbreaks, and its presence does not prevent recurrences.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactivation is not attributed to mutation of the latent viral genome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrences come from latent virus already established in the ganglion, not from acquiring a new strain.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with established genital HSV-2 infection asks how often he might be contagious when he has no symptoms at all. Approximately what proportion of the time do patients with HSV-2 shed virus asymptomatically?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 5-10% of the time

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10-20% of the time

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 30-40% of the time

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50-60% of the time

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 70-80% of the time

explanation.summary: Patients with HSV-2 shed virus asymptomatically roughly 10-20% of the time; for HSV-1 the figure is about 5-10%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick gives these two numbers side by side: HSV-1 is shed without symptoms approximately 5-10% of the time and HSV-2 roughly 10-20% of the time. This is why avoiding contact only with visible lesions does not prevent transmission, and why a patient who feels entirely well can still infect a partner.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 5-10% is the asymptomatic shedding rate quoted for HSV-1, not HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No herpes simplex virus type is described as shedding asymptomatically a third of the time.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This figure far exceeds the shedding rate reported for either HSV type.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 70% is the proportion of genital herpes transmissions attributed to asymptomatic shedding, not the fraction of time virus is shed.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student recovers from an illness with fever, sore throat, and cervical adenopathy. Six years later, while receiving immunosuppressive therapy after a kidney transplant, the same virus reactivates. This virus establishes latency primarily in which of the following cell types?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow progenitor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4+ T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monocytes and tissue macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal tubular epithelial cells

explanation.summary: Epstein-Barr virus establishes latency primarily in B lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV, like other herpesviruses, causes latent infections that can reactivate when the host becomes immunosuppressed. Latency is established primarily in B lymphocytes, although the virus can also be found in epithelial cells and other cell types. This is why immunosuppression after transplantation can allow the virus to re-emerge.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow progenitor cells are among the cells in which CMV establishes latency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4+ T cells harbor latent human herpesvirus 6 and 7, not EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes and macrophages are sites of cytomegalovirus latency, not EBV latency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CMV latent infections are commonly established in the kidneys; EBV does not use renal tubular cells as its principal reservoir.

questions.stem: A laboratory studies how Epstein-Barr virus enters its principal host cell. A viral glycoprotein is shown to attach to a surface molecule that is also known as CR2. Binding to which of the following surface molecules allows the virus to enter the cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD3

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD8

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD19

choices.label: E
choices.text: CD21

explanation.summary: EBV uses a viral glycoprotein to bind CD21 (CR2) on B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV attaches to its target cell through a viral glycoprotein that binds CD21, also known as CR2. CD21 is a surface marker commonly found on B cells, which explains why B lymphocytes are the principal site of EBV infection and latency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD3 is part of the T cell receptor complex and is not used by EBV for entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 is not the EBV receptor; CD4+ T cells are the latency site for HHV-6 and HHV-7.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8 is a T cell molecule and plays no role in EBV attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD19 is a B cell marker, but the brick identifies CD21/CR2 as the molecule EBV binds.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man with no history of infectious mononucleosis asks whether he has ever been infected with Epstein-Barr virus. Approximately what proportion of adults have been infected with EBV and carry antibodies to the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fewer than 10%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 25%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 50%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 75%

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 90%

explanation.summary: By adulthood, more than 90% of individuals have been infected with EBV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most people acquire several herpesviruses before adulthood, and latency is established early. By adulthood, more than 90% of individuals have been infected with EBV and have antibodies to the virus, and many were completely asymptomatic at the time of primary infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This drastically understates EBV seroprevalence, which is near-universal in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A quarter of adults is far below the observed seroprevalence of EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About half is closer to the seroprevalence of CMV by age 40, not EBV in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Three-quarters still understates the greater than 90% figure for adults.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl feels entirely well and has no symptoms, but she is known to be EBV seropositive. Her boyfriend develops infectious mononucleosis three weeks after they begin dating. Which of the following best explains how she transmitted the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerosol spread of virus from the lower respiratory tract

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bloodborne spread of virus from latently infected B lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sexual transmission of virus present in semen and cervical fluid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shedding of virus in oral secretions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shedding of virus in urine from chronically infected renal tubules

explanation.summary: EBV is spread predominantly by oral secretions, and asymptomatic carriers still shed virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV infects the epithelium of the oropharynx and the salivary glands and is shed from these cells, which is why mononucleosis is called the kissing disease. Even asymptomatic patients shed virus to some degree in oral secretions, so they remain infectious and can readily spread the disease to others.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes spread by oral secretions, not by aerosols from the lower airway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latently infected B cells are the viral reservoir, but person-to-person spread is by oral secretions rather than blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Semen is listed as a body fluid that transmits cytomegalovirus, not EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine is a recognized vehicle for cytomegalovirus transmission, not for EBV.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy and his 22-year-old aunt are both infected with Epstein-Barr virus during the same household outbreak. Compared with his aunt, the boy is most likely to have which of the following presentations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blueberry muffin rash with hepatosplenomegaly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Classic mononucleosis with weeks of disabling fatigue

choices.label: C
choices.text: High fever followed by a rash that begins on the trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mild pharyngitis with or without tonsillitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia on the lateral borders of the tongue

explanation.summary: EBV in children usually causes mild pharyngitis, while adults get classic mononucleosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical manifestations of EBV depend on the patient's age. In children, most cases present as a mild pharyngitis with or without tonsillitis, whereas in adults the presentation is most commonly the classic symptoms of mononucleosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A blueberry muffin rash with hepatosplenomegaly describes congenital cytomegalovirus infection in a neonate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Classic mononucleosis is the adult presentation, which is what his aunt would be expected to develop.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High fever followed by a truncal rash as the fever breaks is roseola infantum caused by HHV-6/7.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oral hairy leukoplakia occurs in patients with AIDS and the severely immunosuppressed, not in healthy children.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with serologically confirmed infectious mononucleosis is otherwise healthy and asks how long she will feel ill. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most symptoms resolve in 2 to 4 weeks, but fatigue may last for months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most symptoms resolve within 48 hours of starting antiviral therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Symptoms last 3 to 5 days and end abruptly as a rash appears

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symptoms recur predictably every few weeks for the rest of her life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symptoms usually persist for 6 to 12 months in healthy patients

explanation.summary: Mononucleosis symptoms usually persist 2 to 4 weeks, though fatigue can linger for months.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the majority of patients with mononucleosis, symptoms persist for 2 to 4 weeks. Some symptoms, especially fatigue, may persist for months. Complications of EBV are rare in otherwise healthy patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes no antiviral therapy that truncates mononucleosis to two days.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 3 to 5 day fever ending as a rash appears describes roseola infantum, not mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Predictable lifelong recurrences are not a feature of EBV infection in a healthy host.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Six to twelve months overstates the usual course; only fatigue tends to linger.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with untreated HIV infection and a CD4 count of 90/uL has raised, white, corrugated lesions along the lateral borders of his tongue. Biopsy of the lesions contains herpesvirus DNA. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus esophagitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Roseola infantum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrush

explanation.summary: Oral hairy leukoplakia is an EBV lesion of the lateral tongue seen in AIDS and severe immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: In patients with AIDS and the severely immunosuppressed, oral hairy leukoplakia is a common clinical presentation caused by EBV. Patients present with raised, white, corrugated lesions on the lateral sides of the tongue, and occasionally the buccal mucosa, and these lesions contain EBV DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV esophagitis presents with esophageal symptoms rather than corrugated tongue plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an EBV-associated malignancy of the nasopharynx, not a tongue plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Roseola infantum is a febrile exanthem of young children caused by HHV-6/7.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrush is a fungal infection caused by Candida species and would not contain herpesvirus DNA.

questions.stem: A physician examines a severely immunosuppressed patient with white plaques on the tongue and wants to distinguish oral hairy leukoplakia from thrush at the bedside. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor thrush?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lesions confined strictly to the lateral borders of the tongue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lesions shown to contain viral DNA when a biopsy is taken

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lesions that appeared only as the patient's immunity declined

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lesions that are easily removed from the tongue by light scraping

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lesions with a raised, white, corrugated plaque-like surface

explanation.summary: Thrush scrapes off the tongue easily, whereas oral hairy leukoplakia does not.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrush and oral hairy leukoplakia have a very similar clinical appearance, so a quick scrape test is used to distinguish them before laboratory testing. Thrush can easily be removed from the tongue with light scraping, while the plaque-like lesion of oral hairy leukoplakia is much more difficult to scrape off.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lateral borders of the tongue are the classic site of oral hairy leukoplakia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lesions containing viral DNA point to oral hairy leukoplakia, since thrush is fungal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both lesions can be caused by a weakening immune system, so this does not separate them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A raised, white, corrugated surface describes the appearance of oral hairy leukoplakia.

questions.stem: Two immunosuppressed patients present with white oral lesions, and one of them has just finished a 10-day course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following statements about antibiotic use and these two lesions is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic therapy reliably clears both lesions within several days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both thrush and oral hairy leukoplakia frequently follow antibiotic use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither lesion is related to antibiotic use or to the patient's immune status

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia frequently follows antibiotic use, but thrush does not

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrush frequently follows antibiotic use, but oral hairy leukoplakia does not

explanation.summary: Thrush often follows antibiotic use; oral hairy leukoplakia has no such correlation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both thrush and oral hairy leukoplakia can be caused by a weakening immune system, but thrush also frequently occurs after antibiotic use because antibiotics disturb the normal flora that hold Candida in check. There is no correlation between oral hairy leukoplakia and antibiotic use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics predispose to thrush rather than curing it, and they have no effect on an EBV lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only thrush shows the antibiotic association; oral hairy leukoplakia does not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both lesions are linked to a weakening immune system, and thrush is additionally linked to antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the relationship described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy in the United States is diagnosed with Burkitt's lymphoma, a B cell cancer, and the tumor cells are tested for Epstein-Barr virus. In the United States, approximately what percentage of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with EBV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 1%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 9%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 15%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 40%

explanation.summary: In the U.S., about 15% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are EBV-associated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Burkitt's lymphoma is a B cell cancer that is one of the malignancies linked to EBV. In the United States, 15% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with EBV, a much smaller fraction than is seen in Africa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Less than 1% would make the association negligible, which is not the case.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 5% understates the U.S. association with Burkitt's lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 9% is the figure for EBV-associated gastric carcinoma worldwide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 40% approaches the upper end of the figure for EBV-positive Hodgkin's lymphomas.

questions.stem: In equatorial Africa, roughly 90% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with Epstein-Barr virus, a far higher proportion than in the United States. Coinfection with which of the following is thought to contribute to this difference by causing EBV-infected B cells to proliferate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicobacter pylori

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasmodium species

explanation.summary: Malaria coinfection drives proliferation of EBV-infected B cells and promotes Burkitt's lymphoma in Africa.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Africa, 90% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with EBV. Coinfection with malaria may cause EBV-infected B cells to proliferate, enhancing viral spread and promoting tumorigenesis. HIV infection likewise increases the risk of EBV-associated Burkitt's lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida causes thrush and has no described role in driving B cell proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicobacter pylori is a gastric pathogen and is not the cofactor described for Burkitt's lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-6 causes roseola infantum and is not implicated in Burkitt's lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tuberculosis is not described as a cofactor for EBV-associated lymphomagenesis.

questions.stem: A pathologist surveys gastric carcinoma specimens collected worldwide and tests each tumor for Epstein-Barr virus. Approximately what proportion of gastric carcinomas worldwide are associated with EBV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 9%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 20%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 35%

explanation.summary: About 9% of gastric carcinomas worldwide are EBV-associated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric carcinoma is one of several malignancies linked to EBV infection. Worldwide, about 9% of gastric carcinoma cases are associated with EBV, making it a substantial but minority share of this common cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 1% would make the link trivial, which understates the association.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 5% is below the reported worldwide figure for gastric carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: About 20% is the lower end of the range for EBV-positive Hodgkin's lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 35% substantially overstates the association with gastric carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 3 years ago and remains on chronic immunosuppressive therapy develops generalized lymphadenopathy and hypercalcemia. A peripheral blood smear shows malignant T lymphocytes. His physician explains that the responsible agent is a retrovirus, but one that causes T cell cancer rather than acquired immunodeficiency. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus type 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1

explanation.summary: Retroviridae contains two medically significant human viruses: HIV, which causes AIDS, and HTLV-1, which causes T cell cancers.
explanation.whyCorrect: HTLV-1 is the second medically significant member of Retroviridae. It causes T cell malignancies, most commonly in immunosuppressed patients such as this transplant recipient. The stem specifies a retrovirus producing T cell cancer rather than immunodeficiency, which identifies HTLV-1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epstein-Barr virus is a herpesvirus, not a retrovirus, and it enters cells by binding CD21.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Human herpesvirus 8 is a herpesvirus that causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular tumor of endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV-1 is a retrovirus, but it causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome rather than T cell cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV-2 is a retrovirus, but like HIV-1 it causes progressive immunodeficiency, not T cell cancer.

questions.stem: A student compares HIV with influenza virus and poliovirus. She notes that the latter two viruses complete their entire replication cycle within the cytoplasm of the host cell, whereas HIV behaves differently once a DNA copy of its genome has been produced. Which of the following best describes where HIV replicates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the plasma membrane, using a membrane-bound viral polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: In mitochondria, using enzymes borrowed from the host organelle

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the cytoplasm, in the same way as most other RNA viruses

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the nucleus, after its DNA copy is incorporated into the host genome

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the rough endoplasmic reticulum, before budding from the cell

explanation.summary: Retroviruses are unusual among RNA viruses in that they replicate in the nucleus after their DNA copy is integrated into the host genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase converts the viral RNA into DNA, and that DNA copy is incorporated into the host cell genome, where it remains. Because the viral genetic material now resides in host chromosomal DNA, HIV replication occurs in the nucleus. Most other RNA viruses never enter the nucleus and replicate in the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: New virions bud from the plasma membrane, but genome replication does not occur there.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV does not replicate in mitochondria or use mitochondrial enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes most other RNA viruses; retroviruses are the exception to that rule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The endoplasmic reticulum is not the site of retroviral genome replication.

questions.stem: A researcher purifies virions from the plasma of a patient with AIDS and characterizes the nucleic acid packaged inside the capsid, as well as the virion-associated enzyme required for the first step of replication after entry. Which of the following findings would be expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One molecule of double-stranded DNA, copied by a viral DNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: One molecule of single-stranded RNA, translated directly by host ribosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two copies of double-stranded RNA, copied by a viral RNA polymerase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two copies of single-stranded DNA, copied into RNA by reverse transcriptase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two copies of single-stranded RNA, copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase

explanation.summary: Retroviruses package two copies of single-stranded RNA and carry reverse transcriptase to convert that RNA into DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retroviruses encode their genetic information as two copies of single-stranded RNA. After entry, the enzyme reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA into DNA, and this DNA copy is then incorporated into the host cell genome, where it remains permanently.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Retroviruses do not package DNA; their genome is RNA that must first be reverse transcribed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The genome is present in two copies, and replication requires reverse transcription rather than direct translation alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The retroviral genome is single-stranded RNA, and the enzyme carried converts RNA into DNA, not RNA into RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase works in the opposite direction, copying RNA into DNA.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of newly released HIV virions shows that each particle is surrounded by a lipid bilayer studded with viral glycoproteins. Which of the following is the source of this lipid bilayer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lipid layer synthesized de novo by viral enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: The endoplasmic reticulum membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Golgi apparatus membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nuclear membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The plasma membrane of the infected host cell

explanation.summary: Retroviridae are enveloped viruses, and the HIV envelope is derived from the host cell plasma membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retroviridae viruses have an envelope, and that envelope is derived from the host plasma membrane as the virion buds from the infected cell. Viral glycoproteins encoded by the virus are inserted into this host-derived membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viruses do not synthesize their own lipid bilayers; envelopes are acquired from host membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The endoplasmic reticulum membrane is not the source of the HIV envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Golgi membrane is not the source of the retroviral envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The envelope is taken from the plasma membrane, not the nuclear membrane.

questions.stem: A virologist annotates the complete genome of an HIV-1 isolate. She identifies the three genes carried by all retroviruses, plus additional open reading frames that are not present in other retroviruses. How many genes does the HIV genome contain in total?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eight

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seven

choices.label: E
choices.text: Six

explanation.summary: All retroviruses carry env, gag, and pol; HIV carries 6 additional genes for a total of 9.
explanation.whyCorrect: Every retrovirus has three genes: env, gag, and pol. HIV contains 6 additional genes beyond these three, giving a total of 9 genes. The extra genes encode proteins that help the virus evade and suppress the host immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eight understates the HIV gene count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Four would mean only one gene beyond the three shared retroviral genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seven understates the HIV gene count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Six is the number of additional genes HIV carries, not its total.

questions.stem: HIV carries six genes that are not found in other retroviruses. A researcher deletes all six from a laboratory strain and finds that the virus still assembles infectious particles in cell culture but is rapidly cleared when introduced into an animal host with an intact immune system. Which of the following best describes the normal function of these six genes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They encode proteins that allow the virus to evade and suppress host immunity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They encode the enzymes that copy viral RNA into DNA and integrate it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They encode the glycoproteins that mediate fusion with the target cell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They encode the lipids of the envelope acquired during viral budding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They encode the structural proteins of the capsid, nucleocapsid, and matrix.

explanation.summary: Beyond env, gag, and pol, HIV's six additional genes encode proteins that evade and suppress the host immune system.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV contains 6 genes in addition to the 3 shared by all retroviruses. These extra genes encode proteins that allow the virus to evade and suppress the host immune system, which is consistent with a deletion mutant that assembles normally in culture but is cleared by an intact immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease are encoded by pol, one of the three core retroviral genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp120 and gp41, which mediate fusion, are encoded by env.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Envelope lipids are not encoded at all; they come from the host plasma membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsid, nucleocapsid, and matrix proteins p24, p7, and p17 are encoded by gag.

questions.stem: An immunoblot of disrupted HIV virions identifies three structural proteins: one forming the conical core shell, one bound to the viral RNA inside it, and one lining the inner face of the envelope. Which of the following proteins are encoded by the HIV gag gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 and CCR5, the cell-surface entry proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: CXCR4 and CD4, the coreceptor and primary receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: gp120 and gp41, the fusion glycoproteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: p24, p7, and p17, the capsid, nucleocapsid, and matrix proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease

explanation.summary: The gag gene codes for the HIV structural proteins of the capsid, nucleocapsid, and outer matrix: p24, p7, and p17.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gag encodes the structural proteins used in the capsid, nucleocapsid, and outer matrix, identified as p24, p7, and p17. These are the proteins detected in the described immunoblot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 and CCR5 are host cell surface proteins, not virally encoded products.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CXCR4 and CD4 are host cell surface proteins used for entry, not gag products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp120 and gp41 are encoded by env and mediate fusion with target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease are encoded by the polymerase gene, pol.

questions.stem: A candidate antiviral is designed to bind the HIV docking glycoprotein so that the transmembrane glycoprotein can no longer drive fusion of the viral envelope with the target cell membrane. The two glycoproteins targeted by this drug are products of which HIV gene, and what are they called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: env, which encodes gp120 and gp41

choices.label: B
choices.text: gag, which encodes p24 and p17

choices.label: C
choices.text: gag, which encodes p7 and p24

choices.label: D
choices.text: pol, which encodes protease and integrase

choices.label: E
choices.text: pol, which encodes reverse transcriptase and integrase

explanation.summary: The env gene encodes gp120 and gp41, which mediate viral fusion with target cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Env encodes gp120 and gp41. gp120 is the docking glycoprotein and gp41 is the transmembrane glycoprotein, and together they mediate fusion of the virus with target cells. A drug blocking these proteins blocks entry.

whyWrongByChoice.B: gag encodes structural proteins of the capsid and matrix, not the fusion glycoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p7 and p24 are gag-encoded structural proteins that do not mediate fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease and integrase are pol products that act inside the cell, not at the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.E: pol encodes replication enzymes that act after entry, not surface glycoproteins.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man with HIV has taken antiretroviral therapy without missing doses for 4 years. On routine monitoring, his HIV viral titer has risen 4-fold. Resistance testing shows that the virus is no longer susceptible to inhibition of reverse transcriptase. A mutation in which of the following genes best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A host gene encoding CCR5

choices.label: B
choices.text: A host gene encoding CD4

choices.label: C
choices.text: The viral env gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: The viral gag gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: The viral pol gene

explanation.summary: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease are all encoded by the HIV polymerase gene, pol.
explanation.whyCorrect: The polymerase gene pol encodes reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease, all of which are critical for viral replication. Because resistance has developed specifically to reverse transcriptase inhibition in an adherent patient, the mutation must lie in pol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CCR5 is a host coreceptor and is not the target of reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 is a host receptor; drug resistance arises from mutation in the virus, not the host receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: env encodes gp120 and gp41, which mediate fusion rather than reverse transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.D: gag encodes the structural proteins p24, p7, and p17, not reverse transcriptase.

questions.stem: An investigational antiretroviral blocks cleavage of the large polyprotein translated from HIV transcripts. Virions still bud from treated cells, but they contain uncleaved precursor proteins and are non-infectious. Which of the following HIV proteins does this drug inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gp120 docking glycoprotein

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gp41 transmembrane glycoprotein

explanation.summary: HIV protease cleaves the polyprotein transcribed from viral DNA, a step required for virion maturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease, encoded by pol, cleaves the polyprotein that is produced from viral DNA transcripts. Blocking this cleavage yields particles that still assemble and bud but contain uncleaved precursors and cannot establish infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Integrase incorporates the viral DNA copy into the host genome rather than cleaving proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA into DNA early in the cycle, before any polyprotein is made.
whyWrongByChoice.D: gp120 is the docking glycoprotein that binds the target cell and has no proteolytic role.
whyWrongByChoice.E: gp41 is the transmembrane glycoprotein that drives fusion and does not cleave polyproteins.

questions.stem: A drug under study allows HIV to enter a CD4 T cell and allows a DNA copy of the viral genome to be produced, but prevents that DNA copy from being inserted into host chromosomal DNA. Which of the following enzymes does this drug inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: gp120

choices.label: B
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

explanation.summary: Integrase, a pol gene product, incorporates the DNA copy of the HIV genome into the host cell genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: After reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy of the viral RNA, integrase incorporates that viral DNA into the host genome, where it remains permanently. A drug that permits reverse transcription but blocks insertion into host DNA is acting on integrase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: gp120 is a surface glycoprotein used for docking, and entry is stated to be intact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p17 is a gag-encoded matrix structural protein with no role in integration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease cleaves the viral polyprotein and acts later, during virion maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase makes the DNA copy, which the stem states is still produced.

questions.stem: A man who has had an undetectable viral load on antiretroviral therapy for 10 years asks why he cannot simply stop his medication and why no curative treatment exists. Which of the following best explains why HIV infection is so difficult to cure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase causes a high mutation rate and viral DNA is permanently integrated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The host-derived envelope prevents the immune system from recognizing the virus at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus replicates only in the cytoplasm, where drugs cannot reach it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus spreads only by cell-to-cell contact that antibodies are unable to block.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus stores its genetic information as DNA that host repair enzymes protect.

explanation.summary: HIV resists cure because reverse transcriptase generates a high mutation rate and the viral DNA becomes a permanent part of the host genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase is error-prone, producing a high mutation rate that fuels escape from drugs and immunity. In addition, the DNA copy of the viral genome is incorporated into the host cell genome and remains there permanently, so suppressed virus can rebound when therapy stops.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The envelope is host derived, but this is not the reason cure is impossible.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV actually replicates in the nucleus once its DNA is integrated, unlike most RNA viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV is a bloodborne pathogen transmitted by blood, sexual contact, and vertically, not solely cell to cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HIV stores its genetic information as RNA and must convert it to DNA inside host cells.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with HIV has taken a single antiretroviral agent for 8 months. His plasma HIV RNA level, previously undetectable, has risen to 45,000 copies/mL, and sequencing of the circulating virus shows several new mutations not present at diagnosis. Which of the following properties of HIV best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its capsid shields the genome from host nucleases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its envelope is acquired from the host nuclear membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its genome is transcribed only within the host nucleolus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its protease degrades host DNA repair enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its reverse transcriptase cannot proofread the DNA it makes

explanation.summary: Reverse transcriptase has no proofreading ability, so HIV mutates rapidly and quickly adapts to a single drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase cannot recognize and correct errors as it copies viral RNA into DNA. HIV makes billions of copies of itself in a single day, so even though most of those mutations harm the virus, a few by random chance benefit it. Those mutant viruses spread through the host and become the dominant strain, which is how HIV escapes both the immune response and antiviral therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The p24 capsid packages the viral genome, but it has nothing to do with how faithfully the genome is copied.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The viral envelope is taken from host cell membrane, and its origin does not affect replication fidelity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viral DNA is integrated into host chromosomes, and the site of transcription is not what generates new mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV protease cleaves the viral polyprotein into functional proteins after translation; it does not act on host DNA repair enzymes.

questions.stem: Zidovudine (AZT) was the first drug approved to treat HIV, but patients given AZT alone continued to progress to AIDS. Modern regimens combine several antiretroviral agents. Which of the following best explains the advantage of combination therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined drugs let the host clear integrated viral DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combined drugs restore proofreading by reverse transcriptase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each drug raises the plasma concentration of the others

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple drugs block viral entry into resting CD4 cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus must acquire several mutations at once to escape

explanation.summary: Multi-drug therapy works because HIV would have to accumulate several resistance mutations simultaneously.
explanation.whyCorrect: AZT monotherapy failed because the high mutation rate of HIV let the virus adapt to a single drug quickly and become resistant. When several drugs act at once, the virus must mutate around all of them at the same time, which is far less likely, so viral titers stay suppressed for years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No antiretroviral regimen removes proviral DNA from the host genome; therapy only suppresses viral titers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcriptase has no proofreading function, so there is nothing for a drug to restore.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Raising drug levels is not the reason multi-drug therapy succeeded; resistance, not inadequate drug concentration, defeated AZT alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Therapy does not prevent the reservoir of already-infected cells from persisting, and that reservoir is the problem.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with HIV has had undetectable plasma viral loads for 6 years while taking antiretroviral therapy. He asks his physician whether he has been cured of the infection. Which of the following best explains why he has not?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies to gp120 neutralize but do not kill the virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free virions persist just below the assay detection limit

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drugs suppress only virus replicating in lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Viral DNA is integrated into the genome of host cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral reverse transcriptase stays active within the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: Once reverse transcriptase makes viral DNA, integrase inserts it into the host genome, where it persists for the life of the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: After viral RNA is converted into DNA, that DNA is incorporated into the host cell genome, and every daughter cell made from that cell carries the viral DNA too. Curing the infection would require destroying every cell holding HIV DNA or cutting the viral DNA back out. Therapy can suppress plasma titers below the limit of detection without touching this reservoir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody responses are not the reason therapy fails to cure; integrated proviral DNA is.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The barrier to cure is archived proviral DNA inside cells, not a small residue of circulating virions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antiretroviral therapy suppresses virus throughout the body rather than sparing tissues outside lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzyme activity in the cytoplasm is not what persists; the integrated provirus in host chromosomes is.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with HIV has had an undetectable viral load on antiretroviral therapy for 3 years. She loses her insurance and stops all medication. Which of the following is most likely to occur over the next several weeks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells will clear her integrated proviral DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her CD4 count and viral load will both remain stable

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her plasma viral load will rise rapidly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her viral load will fall further as drug pressure is removed

choices.label: E
choices.text: She will become permanently resistant to all antiretrovirals

explanation.summary: Antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV replication but does not remove the virus, so stopping it causes viral titers to rebound.
explanation.whyCorrect: The virus is still present in the patient's DNA even when it cannot be detected in blood. When therapy is withdrawn, the integrated provirus resumes producing virions and plasma viral titers begin to rise rapidly again. This is the reason continuity of care matters so much in HIV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No immune mechanism removes integrated proviral DNA from infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Suppression depends entirely on continued drug pressure, so neither value remains stable off therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removing the drugs removes the block on replication, so titers climb rather than fall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resistance arises from mutation under drug pressure, not from stopping treatment altogether.

questions.stem: A man with HIV and leukemia underwent a bone marrow transplant to treat his cancer. Years later he has no detectable HIV despite having stopped antiretroviral therapy, making him one of only a handful of people ever cured of the infection. Which of the following features of the donor cells best accounts for this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A donor immune system that excises proviral DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of CD4 on the donor lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous CCR5 delta-32 mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous deletion of the CXCR4 gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preformed IgG against the p24 capsid protein

explanation.summary: The handful of cured patients received marrow from donors homozygous for the CCR5 delta-32 mutation, which blocks efficient viral entry.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV engages CD4 and then a coreceptor, most commonly CCR5. Donor stem cells carrying a homozygous CCR5 delta-32 mutation cannot be entered efficiently by the virus, so the recipient's reconstituted immune system was resistant and the infection was cured. The other cured patients received similar transplants from donors with the same mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No immune system removes integrated proviral DNA from cells on its own.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 is the primary receptor for HIV, and healthy donor lymphocytes express it normally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CXCR4 is an alternative coreceptor, and losing it was not the change present in the donor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibodies against the capsid protein do not block viral entry and cannot cure an established infection.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man who is homozygous for the CCR5 delta-32 allele, and therefore considered highly resistant to HIV, is found on screening to have acquired HIV infection. Which of the following best explains how the virus was able to enter his cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It entered his cells without first binding CD4

choices.label: B
choices.text: It used CXCR4 as its coreceptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It was carried in by integrase rather than by membrane fusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its protease restored function to the mutant CCR5 protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its reverse transcriptase copied the virus into the CCR5 gene

explanation.summary: CCR5 mutations make a person very resistant to HIV, but the virus can still enter using the alternative coreceptor CXCR4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some people carry naturally occurring CCR5 mutations that make them very resistant to HIV infection. The virus is crafty, however, and strains that bind the CXCR4 coreceptor instead can still engage CD4 and fuse with the cell, establishing infection in a person who lacks functional CCR5.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 is the primary receptor for HIV and binding it is required regardless of which coreceptor is used.
